prompt.context: Montachussett Hospital has hired you and your team to investigate consistently rising costs across their medical transportation benefit program. The hospital covers the cost of picking up patients with various afflictions and disabilities and transporting them to their appointments. Transportation is coordinated by a central dispatching system where a scheduler calls taxi companies, wheelchair van companies, and ambulance companies to schedule all patient rides at least 3 days in advance. The hospital has contracts with a limited number of vendors (taxi, van, and ambulance companies) using a blind-bidding rate-card system where vendors do not know each other's prices. The hospital is open to expanding the vendor pool to increase price competition. Trips coordinated on short notice are charged at a significant premium.
prompt.question: Your team has been asked to identify the key drivers of cost creep in the medical transportation benefit program and make strategic recommendations on how Montachussett might save money. Specifically, the hospital is evaluating a technology-based ride scheduling platform to help schedule and track trips, and would like your opinion on whether investing in such a solution would be wise.

clarifying_info.q: How does the hospital pay for these transportation services?
clarifying_info.a: It comes out of a fund of donations given to the hospital by third parties — this is not relevant to the analysis.

clarifying_info.q: What is the duration or distance of the trips?
clarifying_info.a: There is some variation in trip distance; this will be discussed later in the case.

clarifying_info.q: Can the hospital expand its vendor pool?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the hospital is very open to expanding if they can force more companies to compete on price.

exhibits.title: Expenditure by Category ($, millions)
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing total annual medical transportation expenditure from 2013 to 2017, broken out into Category 1 and Category 2 spend. A year-over-year growth annotation of +10% is visible.

exhibits.title: Annual Expenditure by Patient Population, 2017 ($, millions)
exhibits.shows: A table breaking 2017 expenditure into five patient population segments, showing annual spend, number of utilizers, average cost per trip, and total trips for each segment.

framework: Cost drivers: number of patients needing transportation, total distance/frequency of trips, short-notice booking premium
Supply side: number and type of available vendors (taxi, wheelchair van, ambulance), pricing structure (blind rate card), ability to expand vendor pool
Demand side: patient population segmentation by condition, frequency of appointments, geographic spread
Operational efficiency: scheduling lead time (3 days vs. short notice), dispatching coordination, technology enablement
Strategic options: vendor pool expansion, trip pooling/ride sharing, technology platform to reduce short-notice premium

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, what are your overall observations about the trend in total expenditure? What CAGR does this represent?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note total spend grew from $152MM in 2013 to $208MM in 2017 — approximately 6% CAGR over 4 years. Candidate should also identify that costs are split between Category 1 (Emergency/Ambulance) and Category 2 (all other patient types).

steps: 1.368^(0.25) ≈ 1.082 (using rule of thumb: ~8% simple, casebook states ~6% CAGR)

questions.prompt: Using Exhibits 1 and 1B together, which patient populations are the biggest drivers of annual costs? Which demographic in Category 2 is the most expensive to transport on a per-patient-per-year basis?
questions.guidance: Candidate should infer that Category 1 = Emergency/Ambulance ($28MM) and Category 2 = all others ($180MM combined). Wheelchair-bound patients account for nearly half of total program cost (~$99MM / $208MM ≈ 48%). Candidate should compute cost per patient per year for each Category 2 group and identify wheelchair-bound as most expensive. Strong candidate notes that Substance Abuse and Dialysis/Cancer Care together represent ~28% of spend but only ~5% of total utilizers.

math.setup: Annual cost per patient = Annual expenditure / Number of utilizers
steps: Substance Abuse: $28MM / 5,655 = $4,951 per patient per year
Dialysis/Cancer Care: $30MM / 3,581 = $8,377 per patient per year
Routine Check-ups: $29MM / 44,074 = $657 per patient per year
math.answer: Wheelchair-bound patients are the most expensive at ~$11,383/patient/year; Dialysis/Cancer Care second at ~$8,377/patient/year

questions.prompt: What are some reasons for the large discrepancies in annual expenditure across patient populations?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorm — see brainstorming section. Key drivers include frequency of trips, distance of trips, and proportion of trips booked on short notice at a premium rate.

questions.prompt: What are some potential strategies the hospital could employ to help drive down costs on non-wheelchair-bound trips?
questions.guidance: See brainstorming section. Key ideas include ride sharing, trip pooling, expanding the provider pool, and leveraging a live-bidding technology platform.

questions.prompt: Your team has found that 8% of volume across substance abuse, dialysis, and routine check-ups are being booked on short notice (costing 2.5x normal base rates of $22/trip). The hospital has identified a start-up called RoundTrip that can bring this premium down to base rates by opening trip bids to Uber and Lyft drivers. Initial deployment cost is $250k plus a $1 fixed per-trip premium for trips scheduled through this service. What is the total potential savings from adopting RoundTrip?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate current short-notice spend vs. new spend under RoundTrip. Shortcut: total trips across these three categories is approximately 4MM (1.1MM + 3.3MM + 0.2MM); 8% = 320,000 short-notice trips. Strong candidate adds a 'so what' — $10MM savings = ~5% reduction in total program spend. Excellent candidate flags startup risk and suggests a pilot program.

math.setup: Step 1: Calculate current short-notice trip volume. Step 2: Calculate current cost at 2.5x base. Step 3: Calculate new cost at base + $1 premium. Step 4: Net savings = current cost - (new cost + fixed deployment cost).
steps: Total trips in scope: Substance Abuse 3.3MM + Dialysis 1.1MM + Routine 0.2MM ≈ 4MM (using 3.3MM + 1.1MM + 0.2MM = 4.6MM; casebook uses ~4MM as shortcut, yielding 320,000 short-notice trips)
Short-notice volume: 8% × 4MM = 320,000 trips (casebook breakdown: SA 152,000 + Dialysis 88,000 + Routine 80,000 = 320,000)
New rate under RoundTrip: base $22 + $1 premium = $23/trip × 320,000 = $7,360,000
math.answer: ~$10MM in potential annual savings (approximately 5% reduction in total program spend of $208MM)

brainstorming.prompt: What are some of the reasons there are such discrepancies in annual expenditure across the patient populations?

categories.name: Trip Frequency
ideas: Dialysis and cancer care patients require multiple trips per week for ongoing treatment
Substance abuse patients may have frequent counseling or treatment appointments
Routine check-up patients have infrequent visits, lowering per-patient annual spend

categories.name: Trip Distance
ideas: Specialized treatment centers (dialysis, cancer) may be farther from patients' homes
Wheelchair-bound patients may require transport to specialized facilities
Routine check-ups are often at nearby clinics

categories.name: Short-Notice Booking
ideas: Emergency or unpredictable conditions may force last-minute scheduling
Substance abuse and dialysis patients may have variable appointment confirmations
Short-notice trips are charged at a 2.5x premium, significantly inflating costs

brainstorming.prompt: What are some potential strategies the hospital could employ to help drive down costs on non-wheelchair-bound trips?

categories.name: Demand Management
ideas: Encourage patients to confirm appointments further in advance to avoid short-notice premium
Consolidate scheduling of recurring treatment trips (dialysis) into predictable blocks

categories.name: Supply Expansion
ideas: Expand vendor pool beyond current taxi/van companies to increase competition on price
Open bidding to Uber and Lyft drivers via a technology platform
Implement a live/open bidding system rather than blind rate cards

categories.name: Trip Optimization
ideas: Ride sharing or trip pooling for patients traveling to the same facility at similar times
Route optimization to reduce total distance traveled
Bundle multiple patients going to the same destination

categories.name: Technology
ideas: Deploy a ride scheduling platform (e.g., RoundTrip) to automate scheduling and reduce last-minute bookings
Use real-time tracking to improve dispatcher efficiency
Leverage platform to expand vendor pool dynamically

recommendation: Category 2 patients — particularly wheelchair-bound patients — are the primary drivers of rising program costs, accounting for nearly half of total spend despite representing a small share of utilizers. Substance Abuse and Dialysis/Cancer Care together represent ~28% of spend from only ~5% of total users.

Montachussett should proceed with adopting the RoundTrip platform, which can generate approximately $10MM in annual savings (a ~5% reduction in total program spend) by eliminating the 2.5x short-notice premium on ~320,000 trips per year. Given the modest $250k upfront cost, the ROI is compelling.

Beyond short-notice trips, RoundTrip could be extended to all non-wheelchair-bound trip scheduling, further reducing costs by expanding the live-bidding vendor pool to include Uber and Lyft for all eligible trips.
risks: RoundTrip is a startup — scale risk is significant, as the platform would need to handle over 7MM rides per year. A pilot program is advisable before full rollout.
Using Uber/Lyft to transport medical patients creates liability concerns; a patient waiver program or insurance arrangement may be necessary.
Customer experience may vary widely depending on individual driver quality, which could be a concern for patients with medical conditions.

Expanding to Uber/Lyft could drive existing specialty van and taxi vendors out of business or make them unable to compete, which could reduce the supply of wheelchair-accessible and specialized vehicles in the long run.
next_steps: Launch a limited pilot of RoundTrip for Routine Check-up and Substance Abuse trip scheduling to validate savings projections.
Negotiate liability and waiver frameworks with legal counsel before enrolling medical patients on Uber/Lyft.
Conduct a separate analysis on wheelchair-bound patient costs — explore whether dedicated wheelchair van contracts can be renegotiated or whether pooling/routing can reduce frequency of trips.
Evaluate whether RoundTrip's open-bidding capability can be extended to all non-emergency trips to drive further price competition.
